description: PF-041 fix (ADR-027 §2): independently authored acceptance criteria for score_efficacy.py's --judge pass, one entry per effect_id. Written fresh from each effect's real-world DSP behavior, NOT copied or paraphrased from tiered_prompts.json's L0-L4 tiers -- those are generation prompts fed to the model under test, and grading code against the same text that produced it is the exact tautology PF-041 found (L4 scored 2.00/2.00 by construction, 10/10 verified byte-identical). Each entry is a checklist of acceptance criteria a human reviewer would actually check for, not a redescription of the effect. Do not derive future edits to this file from any tier's prompt text -- author independently or the bug recurs.

specs.trivial-01: Acceptance criteria for a stereo gain stage: (1) exactly one exposed gain control, expressed or convertible to decibels; (2) the same gain factor is applied to both channels with no channel-dependent behavior; (3) 0 dB must produce unity gain (output equals input); (4) the control range must cover both attenuation and boost, not attenuation-only or boost-only.
specs.trivial-02: Acceptance criteria for a mute utility: (1) exactly one boolean control; (2) with the control engaged, output is exactly zero regardless of input; (3) with the control disengaged, input passes through with no gain change or added processing; (4) no other parameters are exposed.
specs.trivial-03: Acceptance criteria for mono-to-stereo conversion: (1) accepts a single input channel; (2) produces two output channels; (3) both output channels carry the identical signal at equal, unity gain -- no delay, filtering, or level difference between them; (4) requires no user-facing controls.
specs.trivial-04: Acceptance criteria for a DC blocker: (1) a sustained non-zero (DC) input settles toward zero output rather than persisting; (2) normal audio-rate signal content (roughly 20 Hz and above) passes through materially unattenuated; (3) works identically on both channels of a stereo signal; (4) requires no user-facing controls -- this is a fixed, always-on utility stage.
specs.trivial-05: Acceptance criteria for a polarity inverter: (1) with inversion active, the output waveform is the negation of the input at every sample (peaks become troughs); (2) a bypass control exists that restores the unprocessed signal exactly; (3) magnitude/level is unaffected by inversion, only sign; (4) behaves identically on both channels.
specs.filters-01: Acceptance criteria for a resonant low-pass filter: (1) content well above the cutoff is attenuated substantially more than content well below it; (2) a resonance/emphasis control that boosts the response near the cutoff frequency, audibly distinct from a flat low-pass; (3) the cutoff is user-adjustable across a range spanning from well below to well above the vocal/mid range (roughly two to three decades); (4) the filter's steepness is characteristic of a cascaded multi-pole design (steeper than a single first-order stage), not just one 6 dB/oct pole.
specs.filters-02: Acceptance criteria for a high-pass filter: (1) content well below the cutoff is attenuated substantially more than content well above it; (2) roll-off steepness corresponds to a second-order (two-pole) design, not a single first-order pole; (3) cutoff is user-adjustable spanning sub-bass through low-mid frequencies; (4) no resonance/emphasis peak is required (a plain, non-resonant response is acceptable, unlike a resonant low-pass).
specs.filters-03: Acceptance criteria for a band-pass filter: (1) a center/mid frequency is attenuated the least while content well above and well below it is attenuated more; (2) a bandwidth or Q control that narrows or widens the passband; (3) the center frequency is adjustable across a range spanning bass through the presence region; (4) at a narrow Q setting the passband is audibly narrow (near-tonal), distinguishing it from a shelving or gentle-slope design.
specs.filters-04: Acceptance criteria for a hum-removal notch filter: (1) a narrow frequency region is attenuated substantially more than everything surrounding it (the opposite shape of a band-pass); (2) the notch center is adjustable within the mains-hum region (roughly 40-120 Hz, covering both 50 Hz and 60 Hz supplies); (3) a width/Q control that trades off how narrow versus how deep the attenuation is; (4) frequencies even a few tens of Hz away from the notch center are left essentially unaffected.
specs.filters-05: Acceptance criteria for a high-shelf EQ: (1) frequencies above a corner point are boosted or cut by a controllable amount while frequencies well below the corner are left essentially unaffected; (2) unlike a band-pass or notch, everything above the corner moves together rather than only a narrow band; (3) both boost and cut are available (a bidirectional gain control, not attenuation-only); (4) the corner frequency sits in the upper-mid to high range, appropriate for adding or removing brightness/air rather than bass.
specs.time-based-01: Acceptance criteria for a stereo delay: (1) a discrete, audible repeat of the input appears after a controllable time offset, not a continuous smear; (2) a feedback control that produces multiple decaying repeats, not just one; (3) a dry/wet control that can range from no delayed signal to delay-only; (4) time changes made while audio is playing do not produce a harsh click or zipper artifact (implies interpolated/fractional delay reading, not a hard sample-index jump).
specs.time-based-02: Acceptance criteria for a ping-pong delay: (1) distinct from a plain stereo delay, successive echoes must alternate between left and right output rather than repeating symmetrically or only on the input's own side; (2) feedback and dry/wet controls are present as in a standard delay; (3) the alternation is consistent -- an echo landing on one side is followed by the next echo on the opposite side, not randomly.
specs.time-based-03: Acceptance criteria for a chorus: (1) the effect is built on a short, continuously modulated delay (not a fixed delay), producing pitch wobble/thickening rather than a discrete echo; (2) a rate control for the modulation speed and a depth control for modulation amount are both present; (3) applied to a stereo signal, the two channels sound different from each other (not just doubled), indicating decorrelation between channels rather than an identical mono process copied to both sides; (4) a dry/wet control is present.
specs.time-based-04: Acceptance criteria for a flanger: (1) built on a very short modulated delay shorter than chorus-typical range, producing the characteristic sweeping comb-filter/jet-plane sound rather than pitch-doubling thickness; (2) a feedback control exists and can be driven strongly enough to produce a pronounced, resonant sweep, distinguishing it from chorus (which is not typically feedback-driven); (3) rate/depth or equivalent modulation controls are present; (4) a dry/wet control is present.
specs.time-based-05: Acceptance criteria for a plate-style reverb: (1) the output is a dense, smooth decay rather than a small number of discrete, countable echoes -- this is the structural difference from a delay; (2) a decay-time control that lengthens or shortens how long the tail persists; (3) a high-frequency damping control that makes the tail progressively duller over its decay, not spectrally flat throughout; (4) a dry/wet control is present; (5) output remains stereo.
specs.dynamics-01: Acceptance criteria for a compressor: (1) signal exceeding a threshold is attenuated more than signal below it, with the amount of attenuation controlled by a ratio parameter; (2) attack and release controls shape how quickly gain reduction engages and releases, and changing them produces an audibly different response to transients; (3) a makeup-gain control is available to restore overall level after compression; (4) low-level (below-threshold) signal is left essentially unaffected in gain.
specs.dynamics-02: Acceptance criteria for a brick-wall limiter: (1) output level must not exceed the configured ceiling under any tested input level, including transients -- this is a hard constraint, not a soft tendency; (2) the ceiling is user-adjustable and expressed relative to full scale; (3) the attack response is fast enough to catch short transients (materially faster than a typical compressor's attack); (4) a release control governs how quickly gain reduction relaxes after the signal drops back below the ceiling.
specs.dynamics-03: Acceptance criteria for a noise gate: (1) when input level is below the threshold, output is reduced toward silence rather than passed through; (2) when input level is above the threshold, output passes essentially unmodified; (3) a hold control keeps the gate open briefly after the signal drops below threshold, preventing rapid chatter on a decaying signal; (4) opening (attack) is fast relative to closing (release), matching how a gate is expected to behave differently from a compressor.
specs.dynamics-04: Acceptance criteria for an upward expander: (1) signal below the threshold is made quieter still (pushed further down, the opposite of a noise gate's hard cutoff), rather than being fully silenced; (2) signal above the threshold is left essentially unaffected; (3) a ratio control governs how aggressively below-threshold signal is pushed down; (4) attack/release controls shape the response over time, distinguishing gradual downward expansion from a gate's binary open/closed behavior.
specs.dynamics-05: Acceptance criteria for a sidechain compressor: (1) two distinct signal inputs exist -- a program signal being processed and a separate key/sidechain signal that is NOT itself heard in the output; (2) gain reduction on the program signal is driven by the key signal's level, not the program signal's own level; (3) threshold, ratio, attack, and release controls are all present and behave as in a standard compressor, but analyzing the key input rather than the program input; (4) with no signal on the key input, the program signal passes through with no gain reduction.
specs.generative-01: Acceptance criteria for a sine test oscillator: (1) the output is a single sinusoidal partial with no additional harmonics -- a spectral analysis would show one dominant tone, not a sawtooth/square-like harmonic series; (2) frequency is user-adjustable across the full audible range (roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz); (3) an amplitude control scales output level; (4) requires no gate/trigger input -- it free-runs continuously once instantiated.
specs.generative-02: Acceptance criteria for a sawtooth ADSR voice: (1) the raw oscillator waveform is sawtooth-shaped (a full harmonic series with energy falling off roughly 1/n), distinguishing it from a sine or square source; (2) a gate input triggers note-on/note-off behavior; (3) the four ADSR stages (attack, decay, sustain, release) are each independently controllable and each audibly shapes the amplitude envelope over time; (4) releasing the gate produces a release-stage fade rather than an instant cutoff.
specs.generative-03: Acceptance criteria for a 2-operator FM synth: (1) a carrier oscillator's frequency or phase is modulated by a second (modulator) oscillator, producing sideband frequencies not present in either oscillator alone -- distinguishing this from simple amplitude mixing of two tones; (2) a modulation-index or equivalent control that, when increased, audibly adds more inharmonic/bright content; (3) the modulator's frequency is set relative to the carrier (a ratio), so that changing the carrier's pitch moves the modulator's frequency proportionally rather than leaving it fixed.
specs.generative-04: Acceptance criteria for tone-shaped white noise: (1) the underlying source is broadband noise with no discernible pitch, not a tonal oscillator; (2) a tone/cutoff control audibly changes the brightness of the noise, consistent with a low-pass response (turning it down should make the noise progressively duller, not just quieter); (3) an output level control scales overall loudness independent of the tone control.
specs.generative-05: Acceptance criteria for Karplus-Strong plucked-string synthesis: (1) the excitation is a short burst rather than a sustained tone -- the string decays naturally after being triggered rather than being continuously driven; (2) the decaying pitch corresponds to a delay line whose length sets the fundamental frequency, and frequency is user-adjustable; (3) a damping control changes how quickly the high-frequency content of the pluck decays relative to the fundamental, giving a duller or brighter pluck; (4) requires a trigger/gate to initiate each pluck rather than free-running continuously.
